paper_title: VLA-$Δ$: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$Δ$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$Δ$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $π_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Building generalist robot policies that follow natural-language instructions in diverse environments is long-standing goal of embodied intelligence. Vision-language-action (VLA) models (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Community, 2026; Li et al., 2024a) have recently emerged as promising paradigm toward this goal. Built on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), VLAs inherit rich semantic knowledge and visual understanding from large-scale vision-language pretraining. They use the VLM backbone to encode task instructions and visual observations, mapping these representations to robot actions and achieving strong performance across diverse benchmarks. Despite this progress, VLAs often exhibit failures revealing limited understanding of physical dynamics. For example, policy may close its gripper before reaching the target object, or continue toward the placement location after failed grasp. In such cases, the policy appears to replay memorized trajectory rather than respond to the evolving scene. These failures suggest that reliable manipulation requires reasoning about how the robot and its environment should change as the task progresses. key reason is that most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions and lack explicit supervision of the intermediate physical state changes. They tend to overfit observationaction correspondences instead of capturing how physical states change over time. As illustrated in Fig. 1, existing studies (Li et al., 2026; Cen et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026) introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction to guide action generation by implicitly modeling Figure 1 Comparison of transition modeling paradigms in visionlanguageaction policies. (a) Direct VLA maps observations and instructions directly to actions. (b) Reasoning VLA describes task plans and subgoals in language space. (c) WAM predicts future visual states, while (d) Latent-WAM predicts future latent representations. (e) VLAmodels physical state changes through multilevel supervision. state changes. (b) Reasoning VLAs such as ECoT (Zawalski et al., 2024) autoregressively infer task plans and object locations before generating actions. However, their chain-of-thought supervision focuses on high-level task planning and state reasoning, together with sparse visual localization. It describes what should be done next, but not how the physical states of the robot and objects change between current and future states. (c) World Action Models (WAMs) (Cai et al., 2026) model state changes by generating future images. These methods provide denser visual details, but future-image reconstruction mainly enforces consistency in scene appearance and does not explicitly identify which changes are necessary for task completion. Moreover, generating future images typically introduces additional inference cost. (d) Latent-WAMs (Chen et al., 2026) move future prediction into latent space, reducing the cost of visual reconstruction. However, their latent representations still model only future visual states, rather than signals tied to physical states and motion interactions. Overall, these approaches supervise either high-level task semantics or future visual appearance, but rarely supervise the physical state transition itself, i.e., how object poses, spatial relations, and robotobject contacts change from the current state to the future. Yet it is precisely these physical changes that directly define which actions the robot must take. To bridge this gap, we propose to explicitly model physical state transitions as learning targets. Such transitions should be both linked to task intent and grounded in concrete visual information: task semantics alone cannot specify how objects move, while visual appearance alone cannot indicate which changes matter for the task. Our core design is to extract physical state-transition information between the current and future states, encompassing both task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes. We aim to learn transition representations that capture task semantics while preserving motion details, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. We therefore introduce VLA-, general framework using physical state transitions as explicit learning targets. The framework incorporates learnable Physical State Difference Queries into the vision-language backbone to form unified transition representation conditioned on current observations and task instructions. We shape this representation through two supervision pathways: direct prediction and autoregressive generation. 1 Structured Transition Slots provide structured supervision for variables including spatial positions and contact states, encouraging semantic division of labor among Queries and giving the transition representation clear physical meaning. 2 Optical Flow provides dense visual motion supervision, encouraging the representation to preserve motion details of objects and grippers. 3 Future-State Difference Text provides coherent semantic supervision for task progress, spatial displacement, contact changes, and associated physical constraints through autoregressive generation. Together, these three signals guide the Query representations to jointly encode task semantics and visual motion changes, supporting continuous action generation. We construct pretraining dataset comprising approximately 484 hours and 24 million frames and derive physical state-transition supervision signals from it. The three supervision signals are introduced only during pretraining, while downstream fine-tuning uses only the action-learning objective. This training scheme allows the physical state-transition knowledge acquired during pretraining to provide representational foundation for downstream policy learning and adapt to the continuous control requirements of specific tasks. During deployment, the model directly generates actions without decoding intermediate supervision targets. VLAachieves strong performance in both simulation and real-robot experiments. VLAachieves success rate of 98.40% on LIBERO and outperforms all compared methods under both the Clean and Random settings on RoboTwin. In real-robot experiments, it outperforms π0.5 by 5.5%. These results suggest that physical state-transition supervision during pretraining helps the model focus on task-relevant motion changes, enabling it to benefit from pretrained transition representations during downstream fine-tuning. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. We propose VLA-, general framework using physical state transitions as explicit learning targets. By explicitly modeling task semantics and visual motion changes, it provides more direct supervision for continuous action generation. 2. We curate approximately 484 hours and 24 million frames of robot demonstrations and develop complete automated data annotation pipeline to generate large-scale, multilevel physical state-transition annotations for model pretraining. 3. VLAachieves the highest success rates among the compared methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin and outperforms π0.5 in real-robot experiments.

sections.title: 2.2 Multilevel Physical State Transition Learning
sections.content: Structured Transition Slots Supervision. Physical State Difference Queries lack explicit constraints on their semantic roles when trained solely through action prediction. To encourage transition representations to encode physically meaningful information, we introduce Structured Transition Slots, which organize task-relevant state variables and their changes into nine categories of supervision targets with predefined semantic roles: task progress, task phase, target position, gripper position, motion and relative displacement, interactable position, gripper state transitions, contact transitions, and obstacle risk. This supervision encourages the assigned Queries to develop soft semantic division of labor while preserving information exchange among Queries, allowing them to jointly support action generation. Figure 3 presents an example of Structured Transition Slot annotations for complete manipulation episode. Further details appear in Appendix B.2. We assign subset of Queries to these structured targets. For each slot category, lightweight prediction head reads the corresponding Query hidden representations to output ˆyi. The overall structured objective is Lslot = (cid:80)9 i=1 wi Li(ˆyi, yi), where wi denotes the weight assigned to each target category. These structured targets provide direct supervision for learning key state variables. Dense Optical Flow Supervision. Structured Transition Slots supervise predefined state variables and their changes, but do not fully capture fine-grained visual motion during object movement, gripper approach, and local alignment. To complement this information, we introduce Optical Flow supervision using dense twodimensional displacements between current and subsequent observations from the same viewpoint, encouraging Query representations to preserve local motion details in the image plane. We use lightweight optical flow decoder that reads only the final hidden states of the last Nflow difference queries and decodes their motion information into dense optical flow. The total loss is defined as Lflow = Lall + βmotionLmotion, where Lall is the average error over all valid pixels, and Lmotion is the average error over motion pixels whose target flow magnitude exceeds predefined threshold. Optical flow alone does not distinguish task-relevant motion from other image motion. We therefore combine it with Structured Transition Slots and Future-State Difference Text, jointly constraining transition representations through state semantics and visual motion objectives. sections.title: 2.3 Automated Data Annotation Pipeline
sections.content: As shown in Figure 3(c), we develop an automated annotation pipeline to produce standardized physical statetransition annotations for robot demonstrations from multiple sources. First, we convert all data sources into the unified LeRobot v3 trajectory format. For keyframe selection, we use Qwen3.8 to segment demonstration videos into manipulation stages based on task instructions, identifying processes such as approaching, aligning, and grasping. Stage boundaries serve as keyframe candidates, and additional keyframes are sampled adaptively according to the complexity of the operations within each stage. For semantic annotation, we use Qwen3.8 to generate structured semantic labels. For visual annotation, we use the object descriptions in these labels to prompt SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2025) to obtain bounding boxes and segmentation masks for target objects, grippers, and obstacles. We then use UniDepth V2 (Piccinelli et al., 2025) to estimate image depth and extract depth information near the center of each target object. Finally, we align and integrate semantic and geometric information from current and future time steps according to predefined rules, producing unified physical state-transition annotations and constructing training samples from them. For optical flow annotation, we use MegaFlow (Zhang et al., 2026a) to estimate dense two-dimensional displacements offline between the current and subsequent frames from the same camera view. Quality control is integrated throughout the pipeline. We first use automated checks to identify formatting errors, temporal misalignment, invalid coordinates, inconsistent object identities, and depth anomalies. GPT5.6 then reviews complex cases or conflicting annotations against visual evidence on field-by-field basis and flags uncertain information. Finally, we conduct stratified manual audit to assess annotation quality. We describe the annotation pipeline in detail in Appendix B.3.

sections.content: Implementation and training. VLAis built on the GR00T N1 architecture. The vision-language model is initialized with the weights of ZR-0base (Li et al., 2026). Simulation and real-world platforms. We evaluate VLAon the LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025) and assess its generalization on LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025). sections.title: 3.2 Simulation Benchmark Evaluation
sections.content: LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. We first evaluate the model on LIBERO. As shown in Table 1, VLAachieves an average success rate of 98.4%, the highest among all compared methods. To further evaluate generalization under out-of-distribution environmental changes, we test the model on four perturbation types in LIBERO-Plus: Language, Light, Background, and Layout. Figure 4 LIBERO-Plus performance under four different perturbations. As shown in Figure 4, VLAmaintains high task success rate across all perturbation settings and remains competitive with leading methods. These results indicate that VLAachieves strong performance on the standard LIBERO benchmark without substantially compromising its ability to adapt to changes in visual appearance, background, and layout. Notably, under the Language perturbation, VLAachieves 89.0%, outperforming π0.5 at 82.6% by 6.4 percentage points. This result suggests that the explicit semantic information provided by the Future-State Difference Text enables the policy to rely more on task-relevant state transitions when interpreting instructions, thereby reducing its sensitivity to superficial variations in language. RoboTwin 2.0. We further evaluate VLAon RoboTwin 2.0. As shown in Table 2, VLAachieves average success rates of 90.06% and 89.74% under the Clean and Random settings, respectively, outperforming all compared methods in both settings. These results exceed those of ZR-0, the strongest baseline in both settings, by 1.36 and 1.76 percentage points. From Clean to Random, the average success rate of VLAdecreases by only 0.32 percentage points, compared with 0.72 for ZR-0 and 1.50 for Motus. This indicates that the model achieves higher success rates while adapting effectively to scene randomization. Under the Clean setting, VLAachieves the highest success rates on BlocksRankingSize and HangingMug among all compared methods. BlocksRankingSize requires arranging three blocks by size through repeated grasping, transport, and placement, with successive operations adjusting spatial relations according to earlier placement outcomes. HangingMug involves rotation, regrasping, and hanging, requiring coordinated changes in object poses and transitions among tabletop support, gripper grasping, and rack support. The state reached at each stage influences the conditions for subsequent operations. These two tasks therefore emphasize progressive spatial rearrangement and contact transitions across multiple stages, respectively. The observed gains support our central premise that explicitly learning changes in task progress, spatial motion, and interaction states helps connect task semantics with continuous action generation. Overall, VLAoutperforms the compared approaches that use intermediate reasoning or future visual state prediction on downstream tasks. These results suggest that treating task-relevant motion and interaction changes as explicit learning targets guides action generation more effectively. sections.title: 3.3 Real-Robot Evaluation
sections.content: Figure 5 presents the real-robot platform, task scenarios, and experimental results. We design five manipulation tasks to evaluate obstacle avoidance, long-horizon execution, fine-grained manipulation, spatial reasoning, and generalization under environmental changes. Each task is evaluated over 40 independent episodes, for total of 200 trials. Task success rates are reported in Figure 5(b). VLAachieves an average success rate of 68.0% across the five tasks. On the obstacle avoidance task, it achieves 42.5%, the highest success rate among all compared methods. This result is consistent with the explicit Object Constraints supervision in Future-State Difference Text. These annotations describe obstacles to avoid and object relationships to preserve, helping the model account for manipulation constraints and potential collision risks during action generation. VLAalso achieves the highest success rates among compared methods on the spatial reasoning and finegrained manipulation tasks. This advantage may reflect spatial position annotations in Structured Transition Slots and visual details from optical flow. On the long-horizon execution and environmental generalization tasks, VLAachieves the second-highest success rates. These results indicate continued effectiveness on complex long-horizon tasks and under environmental changes. Overall, the experimental results support the effectiveness of multilevel physical state-transition supervision in helping policies learn task-relevant state changes and their constraints, and translate this information into continuous control in real-world environments.

sections.content: To analyze the contributions of Physical State Difference Queries, Future-State Difference Text, Structured Transition Slots, and Dense Optical Flow, we conduct ablation experiments on LIBERO. We investigate why Structured Transition Slots improve model performance by extracting the hidden states of Slot Queries from models pretrained with and without structured slot supervision and projecting them into two dimensions using t-SNE. The nine slot targets use seven fixed Query groups. Task progress and phase share G12, while gripper state and contact transitions share G78, with separate output branches for each target. Appendix D.1 details the grouping, prediction heads, and supervision objectives. As shown in Figures 6(a) and 6(b), query representations are relatively dispersed without structured supervision during pretraining. With Structured Transition Slots, the query groups form more compact clusters with clearer boundaries. This observation suggests that structured slot supervision enhances the semantic separability of query representations. To examine whether this structure transfers to downstream tasks, we extract the Slot Query hidden states after task-specific fine-tuning on LIBERO. As shown in Figure 6(c), the Slot Queries still form seven compact, well-separated clusters, although fine-tuning uses only the action-generation objective. This indicates that the query grouping structure established during pretraining persists through downstream finetuning, suggesting that the semantic prior introduced by Structured Transition Slots can continue to guide the learning of task-relevant transition representations. Finally, the complete VLAmodel combines all three supervision types, achieving an average success rate of 98.4%. This result suggests that multilevel physical state-transition supervision jointly shapes more comprehensive transition representations, improving task execution. We also visualize query attention distributions over the input images for the complete VLAmodel and the variant without the three transition-supervision signals. In contrast, the model without transition supervision exhibits more diffuse attention and assigns greater attention to task-irrelevant background regions.

sections.title: 4 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose VLA-, general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. Using robot demonstrations from multiple sources, we develop an automated annotation pipeline to construct Future-State Difference Text, Structured Transition Slots, and Optical Flow annotations, supervising transition representations through task semantics, structured state variables, and dense visual motion. These supervision signals are used only during pretraining to learn representations that support downstream policy learning through action-only fine-tuning, while deployment requires no decoding of intermediate supervision targets. Experiments demonstrate that VLAachieves competitive performance on LIBERO and RoboTwin and the highest average success rate among the compared methods in real-robot experiments. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of individual supervision signals, indicating that explicitly learning physical state changes provides an effective representational foundation for downstream continuous action generation.

sections.title: AI use statement
sections.content: Generative AI tools were used for language editing and polishing, translation, LaTeX formatting, compilation troubleshooting, and the retrieval and discovery of related work. AI tools also supported data annotation and quality auditing, including semantic annotation generation, review of ambiguous or conflicting annotations against visual evidence, and bounding-box reference generation for selected audit fields, as detailed in Appendix B.3. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the final manuscript, references, data, results, and claims.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: A.1 Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained vision-language models with robot demonstrations to connect multimodal understanding with action generation. Related research provides complementary foundations for generalist robot policy learning (Brohan et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024a; Wen et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024d; Team et al., 2024; Bousmalis et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024c; Bu et al., 2025a; Deng et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2026; Shukor et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2026). RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023) encodes actions as discrete tokens and jointly trains on robot trajectories and vision-language tasks. This formulation enables semantic knowledge from visual and linguistic pretraining to support robot control. OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) trains an open generalist policy on large-scale robot demonstrations, demonstrating the value of vision-language pretraining for multitask manipulation and policy adaptation. For continuous control, π0 and π0.5 (Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025) combine vision-language pretraining with flow matching to generate continuous action chunks. GR00T N1 (Bjorck et al., 2025) combines vision-language backbone with flow-matching action expert, providing the architectural basis for our model. Action representations and generative policy learning provide complementary foundations for continuous control (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Lipman et al., 2022; Chi et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Pertsch et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). VLAfocuses on explicit supervision of physical changes between current and future states to shape transition representations for continuous action generation. These supervision signals are used only during pretraining, while downstream fine-tuning relies on action supervision. A.2 Embodied Reasoning Embodied reasoning links high-level task semantics with action execution through intermediate plans, spatial reasoning, and grounded representations (Ahn et al., 2022; Belkhale et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024b; Driess et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b; Huang et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026). ECoT (Zawalski et al., 2024) generates task plans, subgoals, and motion descriptions before action prediction, grounding reasoning in the robot state. ThinkAct (Huang et al., 2025) uses goal-completion and trajectory-consistency rewards to learn embodied reasoning and compresses plans into latent representations that guide action policies. ZR-0 (Li et al., 2026) learns cross-embodiment representations through dense embodied chain-of-thought supervision and can skip reasoning generation during deployment. ThinkingVLA (Lu et al., 2026) interleaves forward textual reasoning, future-image prediction, and inverse reasoning within unified autoregressive architecture. Forward reasoning selects subgoal and guides visual forecasting, while inverse reasoning uses the predicted target state to infer spatial relations and action intent. Actions are generated from the combined reasoning context. These methods show how explicit reasoning can relate task goals and spatial information to robot control. VLAfocuses on task-relevant physical changes between current and future states, combining Future-State Difference Text, Structured Transition Slots, and optical flow to connect coherent semantic descriptions with dense visual motion supervision. A.3 World Action Models In robotic manipulation, world action models connect predictions of future observations or latent states with action generation. Broader work on predictive representations and policy learning provides complementary ways to condition actions on anticipated outcomes (Zhen et al., 2024; Cheang et al., 2024; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024a; Wu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2023; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024b; Yuan et al., 2024a). WorldVLA (Cen et al., 2025) unifies action generation and future-image generation within an autoregressive framework, allowing information sharing between policy learning and world modeling. VLA-JEPA (Sun et al., 2026) predicts latent representations of future observations, learning transition information while reducing sensitivity to appearance and background variations. DreamVLA (Zhang et al., 2026b) forecasts dynamic, spatial, and semantic information to guide action prediction. Motus (Bi et al., 2026) unifies understanding, video generation, and action experts, using optical flow to learn latent actions. These approaches differ in whether future information is represented by reconstructed images, latent features, or complementary prediction targets, but all use predictive learning to support action generation beyond the current observation. Generating future images online, however, adds visual-token decoding or video-denoising costs. VLAcombines readable descriptions of task progress, spatial and contact changes, and physical constraints with structured transition slots and dense optical flow supervision. This joint supervision shapes shared transition representation for action generation without requiring future-image or difference-text generation at deployment.

sections.title: B Pretraining Dataset and Data Annotations
sections.content: B.1 Pretraining Dataset To learn visual, language, and physical state-transition representations for robot manipulation, we construct pretraining dataset by selecting demonstrations from DROID, MolmoAct, and RH20T. We first convert all data sources into unified trajectory format, then filter samples based on the completeness of visual observations, language instructions, robot states, and action records. The resulting dataset covers diverse tasks, scene layouts, robot configurations, and interaction types. Table 4 summarizes the scale and collection characteristics of the three source datasets. Table 4 Overview of the datasets used to construct the pretraining corpus. Dataset Frames Hours No. of Tasks Introduction MolmoAct (Household + Tabletop) 1,104,942 30.693 96 Everyday household and tabletop manipulation with Franka robot, covering organizing, cleaning, opening and closing, grasping, and placement tasks; includes fixed external view, second external view, and wrist-camera view. DROID 27,630,375 511.674 49,630 Open-ended everyday manipulation with Franka robots across different data collectors, buildings, and real-world scenes; includes two external views and wrist-camera view. RH20T 3,898,056 108.279 141 Multi-robot real-world manipulation. The Stage05 release subset covers Flexiv, Franka, KUKA, and UR5 across seven configurations, 19 users, and 21 scene IDs; includes two external views, wrist-camera view, and force/torque fields. DROID contains approximately 76,000 demonstration trajectories across 564 scenes and 84 task categories, totaling approximately 350 hours of interaction. We retain demonstrations with complete timestamps, valid visual frames, and continuous action records, prioritizing trajectories that include approaching, grasping, transporting, placing, and releasing objects. These demonstrations increase the diversity of environments, objects, and tasks in the pretraining data. MolmoAct contains over 10,000 high-quality manipulation trajectories covering household and tabletop settings. We extract visual observations, language instructions, robot states, and actions, retaining trajectories that clearly reflect task progress and subgoal changes. These data provide additional information about language conditioning, spatial relations, and multistage manipulation. RH20T contains over 110,000 contact-rich manipulation sequences spanning multiple robot platforms, sensor configurations, and manipulation skills, with modalities including vision, force sensing, and audio. We use its visual observations, proprioceptive states, and continuous action records; the remaining modalities are not directly provided to the policy network. Grasping, pushing, insertion, and release sequences in this dataset provide additional examples of contact interactions, object state changes, and fine-grained manipulation. Figure 8 Physical state-transition annotation examples: currentfuture observation pair with Future-State Difference Text and Structured Transition Slots (top), and slot annotations for loading plate into metal rack (middle) and hanging mug (bottom). The three data sources complement one another in scene diversity, task semantics, and physical interaction. After format standardization and filtering, the pretraining data cover diverse spatial layouts, motion patterns, and manipulation constraints, providing foundation for learning multilevel physical state-transition representations across tasks and robot configurations. B.2 Physical State-Transition Annotations Figure 8 presents examples of physical state-transition annotations. B.3 Automated Data Annotation Pipeline (1) Data Selection Strategy. We select demonstrations with clear goals, valid observations, complete state and action records, and reliable temporal alignment, considering diversity in tasks, objects, scenes, robot configurations, and viewpoints. Operations cover approaching, aligning, grasping, transporting, placing, releasing, pushing, and insertion. For partially corrupted trajectories, we retain continuous, semantically coherent segments and discard records with ambiguous target identities, action meanings, or temporal correspondences. (2) Unified Trajectory Format. We convert all sources to LeRobot v3, organizing instructions, multiview images, proprioceptive states, actions, and timestamps. Time-series data are stored in Parquet and visual observations in videos, with metadata specifying features, frame rates, and trajectory boundaries. We retain source and trajectory identifiers, robot and camera configurations, calibration information, and field dimensions, units, coordinate frames, and validity indicators. Modalities are aligned by timestamps; missing or unreliably aligned fields are marked invalid. (3) Data Cleaning. Language instruction checks. We identify empty, garbled, truncated, or inconsistent descriptions, correcting recoverable instructions and excluding unrecoverable records from language-conditioned training. Language standardization preserves original text and verifies semantic consistency. Future-state difference descriptions remain supervision labels, separate from input instructions. Temporal consistency checks. We inspect timestamp ordering, duplicates, missing frames, and cross-modal offsets. Different video and control frequencies are permitted when reliably aligned. Temporal gaps define segment boundaries. Visual quality checks. We identify undecodable, black, overexposed, blurred, or uninformative views. Brief occlusions are retained when neighboring frames or other views provide evidence; otherwise, affected annotations or segments are excluded. State and action checks. We inspect missing dimensions, non-finite values, jumps, and out-of-range records using sampling intervals and robot configurations. Unclear action types, rotation representations, units, or coordinate frames are not speculatively converted. Trajectory integrity checks. We identify abnormal lengths, duplicates, and truncation, distinguishing valid waiting and sustained contact from recording stalls. When applicable, training and validation sets are split by trajectory before extracting windows to prevent leakage. (4) Adaptive Keyframe Selection and Semantic Annotation. Qwen3.8-27B identifies operation phases from instructions and videos, selecting boundaries and surrounding frames. Sampling is denser for precise alignment, insertion, gripper changes, and contact transitions, and sparser for smooth transport, while preserving task-critical events. Using keyframes and neighboring clips, the model annotates objects, phases, contact relations, interaction regions, state changes, constraints, and obstacles. Annotations distinguish current states, observed future changes, and goals, as well as explicit and inferred constraints. Fields retain object identifiers, timestamps, supporting frames, and uncertainty indicators. (5) Visual Localization, Depth, and Optical Flow Annotation. SAM 3 produces bounding boxes and masks for targets, grippers, and obstacles. Neighboring frames and tracks maintain object identities through similar-instance ambiguity and occlusion. UniDepth V2 estimates depth, summarized by the local median within valid target-mask regions near the two-dimensional center. This measures visible-surface depth, not the objects geometric center. Severe occlusion or unstable estimates invalidate the field. MegaFlow estimates dense two-dimensional displacement offline between current and subsequent frames from the same viewpoint. Frame identifiers and intervals maintain correspondence with transition descriptions. (6) Annotation Integration and Training Sample Construction. sections.title: C Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: C.1 LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus Benchmark overview. LIBERO is simulation benchmark for evaluating knowledge transfer and multitask manipulation in robotics. It includes four task suites, Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long, which assess spatial understanding, object manipulation, goal-conditioned task completion, and long-horizon execution, respectively. The benchmark provides diverse tabletop manipulation tasks with language instructions, covering grasping, placing, moving, stacking, opening, and combinations of these operations. The four suites emphasize different capabilities. Spatial evaluates the models understanding of relative positions, orientations, and spatial relations, such as placing an object to the left or right of another. Object evaluates target identification and object recognition, requiring the policy to select the correct object and perform the specified operation. Goal assesses whether the model achieves the target state specified by language instruction, such as placing an object inside container or moving it to designated location. Long comprises sequences of subgoals, requiring the model to track task progress, execution history, and intermediate states over extended horizons. Training data and fine-tuning. We perform multitask training using demonstrations from all four LIBERO task suites, with total of 1,693 training trajectories. Standard LIBERO evaluation. We evaluate the model on each of the four suites and report both suite-level and overall average success rates. Each task is evaluated over 50 independent episodes, yielding 2,000 evaluation episodes in total. Each episode uses predefined initial scene configuration and random state. The model performs closed-loop control using only the current observations, task instruction, and robot state. LIBERO-Plus generalization evaluation. To assess adaptation to out-of-distribution environmental changes, we further evaluate the model on LIBERO-Plus. We select four perturbation types and evaluate them across all four task suites, running 50 episodes per task under each perturbation type for total of 8,000 episodes. These perturbations preserve the task goals and underlying manipulation logic while modifying the instructions or environment. Language varies instruction wording, sentence structure, or phrasing. Light changes lighting direction, brightness, or color. Background modifies background objects, tabletop textures, or scene appearance. Layout changes initial object configurations, relative positions, or scene arrangements. We use no additional demonstrations from perturbed environments and perform no perturbation-specific fine-tuning for LIBERO-Plus. The model retains the parameters learned on standard LIBERO and uses the same input interface, action space, and maximum execution steps. C.2 RoboTwin 2.0 Benchmark overview. RoboTwin 2.0 is simulation benchmark for dual-arm robot manipulation, focusing on bimanual coordination, object interaction, spatial manipulation, and policy generalization under environmental changes. It includes 50 dual-arm manipulation tasks and supports multiple robot configurations and scene randomization. Scene generation covers diverse object categories and instances, tabletop layouts, backgrounds, lighting conditions, and language instructions. The official dataset provides large object library and multiple structured domain randomization settings. RoboTwin 2.0 provides two main settings. Clean uses relatively fixed scene appearances and object layouts to evaluate basic dual-arm manipulation in standard environments. Random introduces variations in object instances, initial positions, lighting, backgrounds, tabletop layouts, and instruction phrasing to assess generalization under distribution shifts. The tasks involve bimanual grasping, coordinated transport, object arrangement, container manipulation, tool use, and multi-object organization, placing substantial demands on bimanual coordination, temporal planning, and contact control. Training data. We train on 27,500 demonstration trajectories across all 50 tasks. Each task contributes 50 Clean demonstrations and 500 Random demonstrations. Evaluation protocol. We evaluate all 50 tasks under both Clean and Random settings, running 100 episodes per task in each setting for total of 10,000 evaluation episodes. During inference, the action chunk length is set to 16. The policy executes the first eight actions of each predicted chunk before generating new chunk from updated observations, enabling closed-loop control. sections.content: D.1 Structured Slot Heads and Supervision Objectives Prediction head architecture and outputs. Each prediction branch consists of LayerNorm followed by single linear projection: ut,i = Wi LNi (cid:0)zt,g(i) (cid:1) + bi, (3) where g(i) identifies the Query group assigned to target Si, and zt,g(i) is the mean-pooled final Query representation of that group. Depending on the target type, the output is then reshaped, passed through sigmoid function, or transformed using valid bounding-box parameterization. S1 and S2 share the pooled representation but have separate LayerNorm and linear layers. S7 and S8 share both the pooled representation and LayerNorm, i.e., LN7 = LN8, while using two independent linear layers. The remaining branches each have their own normalization and linear projection parameters. The complete module contains nine linear layers and eight LayerNorm layers, with no additional activation function or dropout between normalization and linear projection. Task progress (S1) and task phase (S2) describe task progression through continuous completion levels and discrete manipulation stages, respectively, and therefore share the Query representation of G12. Gripper state transitions (S7) and contact transitions (S8) both describe interaction events during manipulation and therefore share the Query representation of G78. By assigning semantically related supervision targets to the same Query group, we encourage the model to jointly encode task progression and interaction changes while retaining target-specific prediction capabilities through separate output branches. This sharing provides soft semantic division of labor without requiring deterministic one-to-one correspondence between related targets. Table 8 summarizes the outputs of the nine target categories.
